correctness.rationale: The simple socle is m² because the latter is nonzero and is killed by m. For any nonzero ideal I, the last nonzero m^j I lies in its intersection with the socle, so I contains m², also when I=m². A proper ideal lies in m. The action on m/m² factors through k=R/m; thus the quotient subspace lattice gives exactly the nonzero proper ideals, plus boundary ideals 0 and R. Multiplication of lifts is well-defined because m·m²=0, and k-bilinear by taking a lift of the residue scalar and using the same quotient action on the socle. A radical vector lifts into Ann(m)=m², proving perfection with no splitting and including characteristic two. The product vanishes iff W is contained in U-perp, whose dimension is d−a; this yields the stated Gaussian factor even for a or b zero or a+b>d. Summation gives H_q(d); in an ordered tuple, a zero factor or three proper factors makes the product zero. With no zero factors, the counts of nonzero products with zero, one and two proper entries are 1, sG, and choose(s,2)(G²−H); the ordered pair occupies the two positions in their natural order. This proves the formula for all s>=2 with no exclusion on repeats. In d=1 the lattice is the four-ideal chain, giving G=2 and H=3. Direct replay recovers small ideal lattices by sums of principal ideals: characteristic four gives seven ideals and 25/49 for s=2 without a coefficient field, and the two ternary forms each give 15/32 but respectively 3 and 1 nonzero square-zero ideals. It also verifies the refined pair counts and exact s=3,4 probabilities in all three examples. The replay corroborates the proof and is not used to generalize its quantifiers.
residual_risks: No result outside finite commutative local Gorenstein rings of Loewy length exactly three. Repeat samples and inclusion of 0 and R are essential to the stated normalization; the dimension-refined count excludes both extremes.

evidence: Theorem 4.6 counts exponent tuples for chain rings, Corollary 4.7 makes Loewy-length universality explicit; Problem 1 asks about extending universality and Problem 4 about equal ideal lattices. The split-bilinear subalgebra lattice counts isotropic subspaces (offset 5174), not arbitrary ordered orthogonal pairs. For d>1 the free cube-zero truncation has square layer dimension greater than one, and the square-zero probability formula assumes m²=0.
broader_coverage.reasoning: The chain theorem specializes to d=1, not the non-chain cases. An isotropic count corresponds to a diagonal constraint on a pair; it neither states the dimension-refined arbitrary-pair law nor supplies the no-splitting ideal probability theorem.

originality.rationale: The closest probability theorem handles chains (and principal rings via products), overlapping only the chain case here, while the nearest polarity/lattice and graph results address other objects or weaker conclusions. The elementary Gaussian count is not claimed to be original as finite geometry. The distinct supported result is the full ordered ideal-product distribution with no coefficient-field assumption and its form-independence, together with the dimension-refined incidence. No broad assertion about laws of longer rings or discovery priority is established.
residual_risks: Full text of Curtis–Diesl–Rieck was not available from the lawful routes checked; a related annihilator-lattice theorem or an unindexed equivalent might exist.
No originality is attributed to the Gaussian count of subspaces in a fixed perpendicular space taken by itself.

value.rationale: The formula answers a motivated case of the ideal-product universality question beyond chain or principal rings. It identifies exactly what the full sequence forgets: two forms with identical q,d and all tuple probabilities can have different square-zero ideals. The dimension-refined result explains the mechanism, and the lack of a coefficient-field assumption materially expands the class. This is more than substituting parameters in the chain formula.
residual_risks: Universality uses q and d, not Loewy length alone; does not give a classification up to ring isomorphism.
